10720:
A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning in a language. It is the most fundamental building block of words — the point at which, if you break things down any further, the meaning disappears completely.

Take the word "cats." It can be split into two morphemes: cat (the animal) and -s (the idea of "more than one"). Each of those pieces carries its own meaning. But if you broke "cat" down even further into its individual letters — c, a, t — those letters mean absolutely nothing on their own. A morpheme is the smallest unit where meaning actually lives.
Morphemes Are Not the Same as Syllables

This is one of the most important things to grasp, because confusing the two is the most common mistake learners make. A syllable is a unit of sound. A morpheme is a unit of meaning. They are completely different things.

The word "carpet" has two syllables — car and pet — but it has only one morpheme. The word "carpet" names a floor covering, and it cannot be split into two meaningful parts. The fact that car and pet happen to be English words is a coincidence; inside "carpet," those segments mean nothing separately.

Conversely, the word "walked" has only one syllable, but it has two morphemes: walk (the action) and -ed (the signal that the action happened in the past).

The rule is simple: when deciding whether something is a morpheme, always ask — "Does this piece carry meaning?" — never "How does this piece sound?"
The Two Fundamental Types: Free and Bound Morphemes

Every morpheme in any language belongs to one of two categories.

Free morphemes can stand alone as independent words. They do not need to be attached to anything else. The words book, run, happy, door, fast, tree, and blue are all single free morphemes. Each one, as it stands, is a complete and meaningful unit.

Bound morphemes cannot stand on their own. They carry meaning, but that meaning only activates when they are attached to another morpheme. Bound morphemes in English appear almost always as prefixes (attached to the front of a word) or suffixes (attached to the end).

Common prefixes include un- (meaning "not" — unhappy, unkind), re- (meaning "again" — redo, replay), and pre- (meaning "before" — preview, precaution). Common suffixes include -s (plural — cats, books), -ed (past tense — walked, jumped), -ing (ongoing action — running, thinking), -er (one who does — teacher, baker), -ness (the state of being — happiness, kindness), and -able (capable of being — breakable, lovable).

None of these can stand alone. If you said just "-ness" or "un-" in a conversation, they would mean nothing. They are, in the best possible sense, parasitic — they attach to other morphemes and add to their meaning.

One of the most powerful things about morphemes is how they combine to construct words of increasing complexity.

play → 1 morpheme
plays → 2 morphemes (play + -s)
player → 2 morphemes (play + -er)
players → 3 morphemes (play + -er + -s)
replayed → 3 morphemes (re- + play + -ed)
unhappiness → 3 morphemes (un- + happy + -ness)

This is why morphemes are genuinely useful. If you encounter a word you have never seen before — say, "predeterminable" — you can decode it: pre- (before) + determine (to decide) + -able (capable of being). Even without knowing that specific word, its morphemes hand you the meaning.

Beyond the free/bound distinction, morphemes can also be grouped by the kind of meaning they carry.

Lexical morphemes carry real-world, content-based meaning. They refer to things, actions, qualities, and states in the world — the raw substance of what you are communicating. Most nouns, main verbs, adjectives, and descriptive adverbs are lexical morphemes: cat, run, beautiful, quickly. The core idea of a word lives in its lexical morpheme.

Grammatical morphemes (also called functional morphemes) carry structural or relational meaning. They do not describe anything in the world — they tell you how to interpret the grammar of a sentence. The suffix -ed doesn't refer to any real-world thing; it tells you the action already happened. The word "the" doesn't name anything; it signals that you are referring to something specific. Words like the, a, of, and and are grammatical morphemes — they are free (they can stand alone) but their purpose is grammatical, not descriptive.

A useful way to feel the difference: if you removed all the lexical morphemes from a sentence, all the meaning would evaporate. If you removed all the grammatical morphemes, the sentence would lose its structure but remain partially understandable — "Cat sit mat" still communicates something, like a telegram. Both types are essential; one carries the content, the other holds it together.
Allomorphs — When the Same Morpheme Takes Different Forms

The same morpheme can appear in different physical forms depending on the word it attaches to. These different forms of a single morpheme are called allomorphs (meaning, roughly, "other forms").

The clearest example in English is the plural morpheme — the morpheme that means "more than one." It is a single, abstract morpheme, but it is pronounced differently in different words. In "cats," it sounds like a sharp "s." In "dogs," it sounds like a "z." In "buses," it sounds like "iz." Your brain automatically processes all three as the same signal — "more than one" — even though your mouth produces them differently based on what precedes them. Each of those spoken variants is an allomorph of the same underlying morpheme.

Allomorphs can look dramatically different from each other. The plural of "child" is "children," where the morpheme for plurality is -ren, a remnant of older English. The plural of "ox" is "oxen." The plural of "sheep" is "sheep" — no visible change at all.

This brings us to a subtle but elegant concept: the zero morpheme, also called the null morpheme. In words like "sheep" (plural) or "deer" (plural), the grammatical meaning of plurality is clearly there — you know there is more than one — but there is no visible or audible form to represent it. The morpheme is present in terms of meaning, but its physical form is nothing, zero.

Similarly, in English the present tense of a verb for I, you, and they requires no ending: "I run," "you run," "they run." There is a grammatical signal for tense, but it takes no visible form. Linguists argue that this "absence" is itself meaningful — the zero morpheme is a real grammatical unit that simply happens to be silent and invisible.

A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning in a language. It is not a letter, not a syllable, and not always a whole word — it is the atom of meaning from which words are assembled.

Free morphemes stand alone as words. Bound morphemes must attach to something else and appear as prefixes or suffixes. Lexical morphemes carry content; grammatical morphemes carry structure. A single morpheme can appear in different physical forms depending on context — those variants are allomorphs. And sometimes, a morpheme carries meaning without having any physical form at all — that is the zero morpheme.

Morphemes are the reason you can decode an unfamiliar word, the reason languages can coin new words effortlessly, and the reason a small set of building blocks can generate the enormous, seemingly endless variety of human expression.
10721:
Morphology is the study of the shape, form, and structure of something — and also refers to the actual shape, form, and structure that results from that study.

Think of it this way: whenever someone asks "What does this thing look like, and how is it put together?" — the answer to that question is morphology.

The word is used across several different fields of study. In each field, the core idea stays the same, but it gets applied to a different subject. Here is what it means in each major context.

This is one of the most common uses of the word. In linguistics, morphology is the branch of grammar that studies the internal structure of words — meaning, how words are built from smaller pieces.

Those smallest meaningful pieces of a word are called morphemes. A morpheme is the tiniest unit in a word that still carries meaning. You cannot break a morpheme down any further without destroying its meaning.

Take the word "unhappiness" as an example. It looks like one big word, but it is actually made of three morphemes stacked together:

  • un- → a prefix meaning "not"
  • happy → the root word, meaning the emotion
  • -ness → a suffix meaning "the state or quality of being something"

Put them together: the state of not being happy. Each piece did a specific job.

Linguistic morphology studies questions like:

  • How do words change when we make them plural? (dog → dogs)
  • How do verbs change to show past tense? (walk → walked)
  • What happens when we add a prefix or suffix to a word? (happy → unhappy → unhappiness)
  • What is the smallest meaningful unit hiding inside a word?

A linguist studying morphology is a bit like a mechanic taking apart an engine — not to break it, but to understand exactly what role each part plays in making the whole thing work.
2. In Biology (The Study of Living Things)

In biology, morphology is the study of the physical form and structure of living organisms — their shape, size, color, and the way their body parts are arranged.

It covers two layers:

  • External morphology — the outer appearance of an organism. For example: the shape of a bird's beak, the pattern on a butterfly's wings, the texture of a plant's leaf.
  • Internal morphology (also called anatomy) — the structure of what is inside an organism. For example: the shape of a heart, the layout of bones, the arrangement of organs.

A classic example: scientists studying the morphology of Darwin's finches look closely at the shape and size of each bird's beak. The beak's form reveals a great deal — what the bird eats, which environment it adapted to, and how it evolved over millions of years.

One important distinction to know: morphology is not the same as physiology. Physiology asks how body parts function (how a heart pumps blood). Morphology asks what those parts look like and how they are structured (what the heart's chambers look like and how they are arranged). Form vs. function — morphology cares about form.

In geology and physical geography, morphology — often specifically called geomorphology — refers to the study of the physical features of the Earth's surface: mountains, valleys, rivers, coastlines, plains, cliffs, and other landforms.

It studies their shapes, how they were formed (by forces like water, wind, ice, and tectonic movement), and how they change over time.

For example: describing the morphology of a river delta means describing how the delta is shaped — how wide it spreads, how the water channels branch out, and what the overall structure of the land looks like where the river meets the sea.

In medicine, morphology refers to the shape and structure of cells, tissues, and organs. Doctors, pathologists, and scientists examine morphology under a microscope to identify diseases, abnormalities, and infections.

For example: when a doctor examines a blood sample, they look at the morphology of red blood cells. A healthy red blood cell is round and disc-shaped with a slightly sunken center. But if those cells look crescent- or sickle-shaped instead, that tells the doctor the patient has sickle cell disease — a condition that is literally diagnosed by looking at the shape (i.e., morphology) of cells.
The Two Ways the Word Is Used

This is a subtle but important point. Morphology functions in two related ways:

  1. As the act of studying — the branch of knowledge or science dedicated to examining form and structure.
    "Morphology is a major area of study in biology."
  2. As the actual form and structure itself — the physical shape or arrangement of something, as a feature or characteristic.
    "The morphology of the coastline changed after the storm."
    "The morphology of the word 'kindness' includes a root and a suffix."

In the first use, morphology is the lens you use to look at something. In the second use, it is the thing you see when you look through that lens.

No matter which field uses the word, the question morphology always answers is:

"What does this look like, and how is it built?"

Whether the subject is a word, a creature, a landscape, or a single cell — morphology is the study of its form and structure, and also the term for that form and structure itself.
10722:
A morsel is a very small piece or amount of something — most often food, but also used for other things in everyday English.

The key idea locked inside this word is smallness, and often pleasantness. A morsel isn't just any small piece — it tends to suggest something that is either enjoyable, precious, or carefully noticed because of how little of it there is.

In its most common use, a morsel refers to a tiny bit of food — the kind you could fit in one small bite, or even less.

Think of a single small piece of bread torn from a loaf, a tiny chunk of cheese, or one little bite of a dessert. That is a morsel. It is not a slice, not a portion, not a serving — it is much smaller than all of those. It sits right at the bottom of the size scale.

Examples:

  • She was so nervous before the interview that she could barely eat a morsel.
  • He picked up a morsel of cake with his fork and tasted it slowly.
  • The dog waited patiently under the table, hoping for a morsel to fall.
  • Not a single morsel of food was left on the plate by the end of the meal.

Notice how in all these sentences, the word draws your attention to how small and limited the amount is. It can suggest that someone is eating very little (out of nerves, poverty, or restraint), or simply that a piece of food is tiny in size.

English speakers also use morsel beyond food, to describe a very small amount of anything — especially something abstract or desirable.

You will often hear or read phrases like:

  • a morsel of information — meaning a tiny bit of information, not a full explanation
  • a morsel of truth — a tiny fragment of truth hidden inside something
  • a morsel of comfort — a small but meaningful moment of relief
  • a morsel of gossip — a tiny, juicy piece of news

The figurative use always keeps the two core qualities: smallness and some degree of value or interest. You would not normally say "a morsel of boredom" — the word naturally gravitates toward things that feel somewhat worthwhile, precious, or appetizing (even when the topic is not food).
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Morsel is a gentle, slightly elegant word. It does not feel harsh or clinical. It often appears in literary writing, careful descriptions of food, or whenever a writer wants to emphasize scarcity — that something is in very short supply.

It can carry a tone of:

  • Scarcity — He had not eaten a morsel in two days.
  • Delicacy or savoring — She tasted every morsel slowly, eyes closed.
  • Withholding — He refused to share even a morsel of what he knew.

When used with negatives ("not a morsel," "not a single morsel"), it becomes a powerful way to say that there is absolutely nothing left — zero, completely empty.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different feel:

Morsel vs. Piece — A piece is neutral and can be any size. A morsel is always specifically small, and carries more warmth and imagery.

Morsel vs. Crumb — A crumb is even tinier, and often suggests something almost worthless or accidental (the crumbs left behind). A morsel feels slightly more deliberate and slightly more satisfying — it is small, but it is still something.

Morsel vs. Bite — A bite refers to the action of biting or the amount taken in one bite. A morsel is the piece itself, and can be smaller than what you'd even call a full bite.

Morsel vs. Tidbit — Both are small and pleasant. "Tidbit" is used almost exclusively for information or gossip in modern English, and sounds more casual. "Morsel" works for both food and information, and sounds slightly more refined.

Morsel is almost always used to mean small. Unlike some words that can shift in size depending on context, a morsel is reliably tiny. If someone hands you "a morsel" of something, do not expect a generous amount.

Morsel is a countable noun. You say a morsel, one morsel, two morsels, several morsels — not "morsel of bread" without an article. You would say a morsel of bread or a few morsels of bread.

It is not a rude or negative word. Even when used to highlight scarcity, morsel itself is not an insult. Compare: "He shared a morsel of his wealth with the poor" — this criticizes the action (sharing very little), but the word morsel itself is neutral and even slightly poetic.

A morsel is a very small piece or amount of something — typically food, but also used for information, truth, comfort, and other desirable things. It always signals smallness, and usually implies that what little there is carries some value or pleasantness. It is a gentle, refined word that fits both everyday conversation and literary writing, and it becomes especially powerful when used with negatives to mean that there is nothing at all left.
10723:
Mortal means "subject to death." If something is mortal, it will die — it cannot live forever. The word is most commonly used as the opposite of immortal (which means living forever, never dying).

Think of it this way: every human being, every animal, every living creature on Earth is mortal. Gods, in mythology and religion, are often imagined as immortal — they never die. But humans? We are mortal. Our lives will end. That is the central truth this word captures.
All the Key Meanings, One by One

1. Capable of dying / Not living forever

This is the most fundamental meaning.

"All human beings are mortal."

It simply states a fact: humans die. They are not built to last forever. When you call something mortal, you are recognizing that it has a limited lifespan.

This meaning often carries a slightly heavy, philosophical weight. When a writer says "he was reminded of his mortal nature," they mean he was reminded that he will one day die.

2. Causing death / Deadly

Here, mortal describes something that results in death — a wound, a blow, or an injury that kills.

"The soldier suffered a mortal wound." — the wound killed him.
"The poison was mortal." — it was lethal, it caused death.

The key test: if something is described as mortal in this sense, it doesn't just hurt — it kills. A mortal blow is a final blow. There is no coming back from it.

3. Relating to death itself (not causing it, but connected to it)

Sometimes mortal is used to describe things that belong to the world of death or the physical, dying body — not necessarily something that causes death, but something that is associated with death.

The clearest example is the phrase:

"mortal remains"

This means a person's dead body — what is left behind after they die. The body is the "mortal" part of a person (the part that dies), as opposed to the soul, which many traditions believe is immortal.

4. Extreme, overwhelming — especially describing fear

This is a very common use in everyday English. Here, mortal is used to intensify an emotion, especially fear or terror, to convey that it is so extreme it feels like your life is in danger.

"She was in mortal fear."
"He was struck with mortal terror."

It does not literally mean she was dying of fear. It means her fear was at the maximum possible level — the kind of fear you feel when you genuinely believe you might die. Think of the most intense, bone-deep fear imaginable. That's mortal fear.

5. Relating to a fight or conflict that goes all the way to death

"mortal combat" — a fight where the goal or outcome is death.
"They were mortal enemies."

A mortal enemy is not just someone you dislike. It is someone whose hatred for you (or yours for them) is so deep and total that it can only end with one of you being destroyed. The enmity is absolute — it lasts until death.

Similarly, mortal combat is a battle fought to the death, with no mercy and no stopping until one side is finished.

6. In religion — Mortal sin

In Catholic Christianity and some other traditions, a mortal sin is the most serious kind of sin — one so grave that it is considered to cause the spiritual death of the soul, cutting the person off from God completely. It is contrasted with a venial sin, which is less serious and more forgivable.

"He confessed his mortal sins."

The word mortal here carries the same idea: something that kills — but spiritually, not physically.

7. Of or belonging to the human world (as opposed to the divine)

This meaning shows up especially in literature, mythology, and poetic writing. Here, mortal is used to describe anything that belongs to the realm of human beings — fragile, earthly, temporary things — as opposed to divine, eternal, or supernatural things.

"No mortal hand could have built this." — no human being could have done it.
"Beyond mortal understanding." — beyond what any human mind can grasp.

Here, mortal essentially means human — with the implication that being human comes with limitations: you are not all-powerful, not all-knowing, and not eternal.
The Single Thread Running Through All Meanings

No matter which meaning you encounter, there is always one idea underneath all of them:

Mortal = belonging to the world of death, dying, and human limitation.

  • A mortal being will die.
  • A mortal wound causes death.
  • Mortal remains are what death leaves behind.
  • Mortal fear is fear at the level of death.
  • A mortal enemy is one whose hatred is deadly and total.
  • A mortal sin spiritually kills.
  • A mortal hand is a limited, human hand.

The thread is always the same: death, limitation, and the fragile, temporary nature of living things.

MortalImmortal
Will dieLives forever
LimitedLimitless
Human / earthlyDivine / eternal
TemporaryPermanent

Actually, let me put that in plain words instead:

If you understand immortal — something that never dies, that lasts forever, like the gods of ancient myth — then mortal is simply its opposite. Mortal things are everything immortal things are not: they end, they fade, they die.
How to Know Which Meaning Applies

When you see the word mortal, ask yourself: what is it describing?

  • A living being? → It means that being will die someday. (mortal creature, mortal men)
  • A wound or blow? → It means that injury will kill. (mortal wound, mortal blow)
  • A dead body? → It refers to the physical remains. (mortal remains)
  • An emotion like fear? → It means the emotion is extreme and overwhelming. (mortal dread)
  • An enemy or conflict? → It means the hatred or battle is absolute, to the death. (mortal enemy, mortal combat)
  • A religious context? → It refers to a sin that spiritually kills. (mortal sin)
  • A comparison to gods or divine power? → It simply means human, limited, earthly. (no mortal could...)

In every case, death — literal or figurative — is nearby.
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine two characters in a story: a god and a human. The god cannot be killed. The human can. The human lives under the shadow of death — every day, every choice, every fear is colored by the fact that life will end. That human is mortal. Everything about them — their body, their wounds, their fears, their sins, their enemies — can be described with the word mortal, because everything about them exists inside the boundary that death creates.

That is what mortal means.
10724:
A mortal is a human being — but not just any ordinary reference to a person. The word specifically highlights one defining truth about humans: we will all die someday. That is the entire point of the word. When someone calls a person "a mortal," they are saying: this is a creature that lives, but will not live forever.

Think of it this way — the word "mortal" comes from the idea of death being unavoidable. A mortal is simply a being for whom death is certain.
Why Use "Mortal" Instead of Just "Person" or "Human"?

Good question. The word "mortal" is not used in everyday casual conversation the way "person" or "human" is. Instead, it is used in specific situations where the contrast between humans and something greater — like gods, immortals, or supernatural beings — is the whole point.

In other words, the word only truly makes sense when there is something immortal (something that never dies) being compared against something that can die.

For example:

  • In myths and ancient stories, gods live forever. Humans do not. So the gods would look down at humans and call them "mortals."
  • In fantasy stories, an immortal vampire or an all-powerful wizard might refer to ordinary humans as "mortals" — beings who age and die while the immortal does not.

So the noun "mortal" is almost always used in a context where mortality (the fact of dying) is being pointed out, often by contrast.

Referring to all of humanity collectively:

"The gods cared little for the suffering of mortals."

Here, "mortals" means all human beings — the entire human race — seen from the perspective of divine or immortal beings looking down at them.

Referring to a single human being:

"He was just a mortal; he could not escape death."

Here, "a mortal" means one ordinary human person, with the emphasis being on their human limitation — the fact that they are not a god, not a supernatural being, not immortal.

Used with a tone of pity, superiority, or drama:

"You are a mere mortal. What can you possibly do against me?"

This is a common line in fantasy, mythology, or dramatic storytelling, spoken by a powerful or immortal character to a human, highlighting the human's weakness and finite lifespan.

Used with humility (even self-referentially):

"I'm just a mortal — I can't do the impossible."

Here, a person uses the word to describe themselves, humbly acknowledging their human limits.
The Feeling and Tone the Word Carries

The word "mortal" as a noun is not neutral. It carries weight. It sounds formal, dramatic, and literary. It belongs more to poetry, mythology, epic storytelling, religious writing, and fantasy than to everyday speech.

When a writer or speaker chooses the word "mortal" over "human" or "person," they are doing so deliberately — to remind the listener or reader of human fragility, limitation, and the shadow of death that hangs over every human life.

It is a word that makes you feel the smallness of human existence when placed against something vast, eternal, or divine.

The plural "mortals" refers to human beings as a group — often used to mean all of humanity, especially when viewed from an outside or higher perspective.

"The immortal sorceress watched mortals come and go like the seasons."
What "Mortal" as a Noun Does NOT Mean

It is important to know what the word does not mean in its noun form:

  • It does not mean a dead person. A mortal is a living human being — one who will die eventually, but is alive right now.
  • It does not mean a weak or cowardly person specifically. It simply means a human being who is subject to death, regardless of how strong or brave they are.
  • It is not an insult on its own, though it can be used condescendingly by an immortal or powerful character toward a human.

A mortal (noun) = a human being, specifically described as one who will inevitably die — often used in contrast to gods, immortals, or supernatural beings.

That is the whole meaning. Everything else above is just the full picture of how, when, and why it is used.
10725:
A mortal enemy is a person, group, or force that is in deep, total, and unrelenting opposition to you — one whose hostility toward you is so extreme that it is considered permanent and absolute. It is not just someone who dislikes you or disagrees with you. It is someone whose very existence is in direct and irreconcilable conflict with yours.

The plural form is mortal enemies.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

To truly understand the phrase, it helps to understand the job each word is doing.

"Enemy" means someone who is actively against you — someone who wishes you harm, works to defeat you, or stands in opposition to you. An enemy is not a stranger who ignores you. An enemy is someone who is against you.

"Mortal" in this phrase is an adjective that intensifies the word "enemy" to the highest possible degree. It carries two powerful meanings at once:

  • "To the death" — the conflict is so serious it could end in destruction or ruin.
  • "Absolute and total" — the hatred or opposition is complete, not partial. There is no middle ground, no possibility of peace, and no soft edges.

Together, mortal enemy means an enemy of the most extreme, permanent, and deadly kind.
What Makes Someone a Mortal Enemy (and Not Just an Enemy)?

Think of it like a scale of opposition:

Rival → Opponent → Enemy → Mortal Enemy

Each step is more serious than the last. Here is how they differ:

  • A rival competes with you but may respect you and there is no deep hatred.
  • An opponent disagrees with you or works against you in a specific context.
  • An enemy actively wishes you harm or works to defeat you.
  • A mortal enemy does all of that — but with total commitment, deep hatred, and permanence. The conflict between you is not a temporary argument. It is a defining feature of both your lives.

A mortal enemy is not just someone you fight with today. It is someone whose opposition to you feels like it will never end, and can never be resolved through compromise or forgiveness.

The phrase is used in two ways — literally and figuratively.

Literally, a mortal enemy is someone who genuinely wants to destroy you, defeat you entirely, or cause your death. This is how it is used in wars, historical rivalries, and serious conflicts where lives are at stake.

Example: "For centuries, the two kingdoms were mortal enemies — they fought to wipe each other off the map."

Figuratively (and this is far more common in everyday language), a mortal enemy is someone whose opposition to you is simply the most extreme and absolute it can be — even if no one is actually being killed. The word "mortal" is being used to express intensity, not necessarily physical danger.

Example: "Those two companies are mortal enemies. They will do absolutely anything to destroy each other in the marketplace."

Example: "She and her sister used to be mortal enemies as teenagers, but now they get along fine." (Here it is used with slight humor or exaggeration to mean they intensely disliked each other.)
Key Characteristics of a Mortal Enemy

Whenever you see or use this phrase, these qualities are almost always implied:

  1. Deep, intense hatred or opposition — not mild dislike, but something burning and profound.
  2. Permanence — this is not a temporary falling-out. The enmity is seen as long-lasting, possibly lifelong.
  3. Irreconcilability — there is no expected resolution. Peace between mortal enemies feels impossible.
  4. Totality — the opposition covers everything. It is not conflict in one specific area; it is a complete and all-encompassing clash.
  5. High stakes — something important is at risk: power, survival, beliefs, identity, or dominance.

Yes. One person can consider another their mortal enemy even if the feeling is not perfectly mutual. However, in most uses of the phrase, the enmity is understood to be mutual — both sides deeply oppose each other.
Real-World Examples to Cement the Idea

• In history: Two rival empires who fought across centuries to destroy each other's power and dominance were mortal enemies.
  • In fiction: Classic storytelling is full of mortal enemies — a hero and a villain who are locked in an endless, defining struggle. Think of any great superhero and their greatest villain.
  • In nature: Prey and predator species are sometimes poetically called mortal enemies because their relationship is one of survival — one lives, the other dies.
  • In everyday life (figurative): Two neighbors who have been in bitter, unresolved conflict for decades, each trying to make the other's life miserable, might jokingly or seriously be called each other's mortal enemies.
  • In politics or ideology: Two groups who hold completely opposite beliefs and see each other as a fundamental threat to their way of life are often described as mortal enemies.

• A mortal enemy is not just someone you are annoyed with or had a bad experience with.
  • A mortal enemy is not a temporary rival you might one day reconcile with (though in fiction, former mortal enemies sometimes do reconcile — which is always treated as a dramatic, remarkable event).
  • A mortal enemy is not a casual competitor. The word "mortal" lifts the phrase far above ordinary competition.
The Emotional Weight of the Phrase

When someone calls another person their "mortal enemy," it signals something heavy and serious. It tells you that this is not just conflict — it is the defining conflict. It says: "This person and I are fundamentally opposed, and that will not change."

Even when used with humor or exaggeration in everyday speech (like saying "broccoli is my mortal enemy"), the phrase works because everyone understands it means total, absolute, and unrelenting opposition — which is exactly what makes it powerful, dramatic, and vivid.
10726:
Mortality is the word that names one of the most fundamental truths about life: every living thing will eventually die. No human, animal, or plant lives forever. That unavoidable, universal condition — the fact that all living beings are temporary — is what mortality captures.

The simplest way to think about it: if something is mortal, it can and will die. Mortality is the noun that names that state of being. It is the condition of being mortal.

Its direct opposite is immortality — the state of living forever, which exists only in myths, religion, or fiction.

Mortality is used in two distinct but related ways: one is philosophical and personal, and the other is statistical and technical. Both are equally important to understand.

Meaning 1 — The Condition of Being Destined to Die

This is the deeper, more personal sense of the word. It refers to the universal human condition of being temporary — of existing as a living thing that will one day cease to exist.

This meaning is most often used in emotional, philosophical, literary, or spiritual contexts. It's not simply about the act of dying; it is about the awareness and significance of being a temporary being in the world.

Examples:

  • "The car accident made him confront his own mortality."

Here, he was suddenly and powerfully reminded that he, too, will die one day.

  • "Great thinkers throughout history have wrestled with human mortality."

Here, philosophers have long grappled with what it means that humans are not permanent.

  • "She felt a sharp sense of her mortality as she held her newborn child."

Here, becoming a parent made her deeply aware of her own limited time.

Notice the phrase "one's own mortality" — this is one of the most common ways the word is used. It means a personal, often sudden awareness that you yourself will die. People are said to "face," "confront," or "come to terms with" their mortality — usually after a health scare, a loss of a loved one, or another life-altering moment.

Meaning 2 — The Rate or Number of Deaths (Statistical Use)

This is the technical, measurable sense of the word, used heavily in medicine, public health, science, and statistics. Here, mortality refers to how frequently or in what numbers people (or animals) die — within a specific group, time period, place, or from a specific cause.

This is where you will encounter the following common terms:

  • Mortality rate — the number of deaths per a set number of people (for example, per 1,000 or per 100,000) within a given time. It is a measurement that tells you how deadly a disease, condition, or period is.
  • Infant mortality — the rate of deaths among babies, typically those under one year of age. It is a key measure used to judge the health standards of a country.
  • Maternal mortality — the rate of deaths among mothers during pregnancy, childbirth, or shortly after.
  • Child mortality — the death rate among children, usually under five years old.

Examples:

  • "The mortality rate from the disease dropped sharply after the vaccine was introduced."

Here, fewer people were dying from the disease per thousand — the proportion of deaths fell.

  • "Infant mortality remains high in regions with limited access to clean water."

Here, a large number of babies are dying relative to those born.

  • "The study examined cancer mortality across different age groups."

Here, researchers were studying the pattern of cancer-related deaths.

You may also occasionally see the plural form mortalities in highly technical writing, referring to multiple categories or recorded instances of deaths across different groups.
Mortality vs. Death — What Is the Difference?

These words are closely connected but are not interchangeable, and understanding the difference will sharpen your use of both.

  • Death is the specific event — the moment when a living thing stops living. It is concrete, singular, and immediate. "Her death was unexpected."
  • Mortality is the broader condition or pattern — the general fact of dying, or the frequency with which dying occurs. "Human mortality is universal."

Think of it this way: death is a single raindrop; mortality is the fact that it always rains. One is an event; the other is the condition that makes such events inevitable.

Similarly in statistics: you would say "There were 200 deaths this year" (specific count), but "The mortality rate was 4 per 1,000" (a proportional measure of death frequency).
The Emotional and Philosophical Weight of the Word

It is worth noting that mortality is not a neutral word. It carries weight. When writers, philosophers, doctors, or ordinary people use it, there is an implicit acknowledgment of something serious and profound — the limits of life itself.

In religion and philosophy, mortality is often contrasted with the soul's potential for eternal life. Many belief systems place great importance on how humans respond to, cope with, or transcend mortality.

In literature and art, mortality is a central theme — think of poetry about aging, novels about illness, or films about legacy. The word appears wherever people grapple with what it means to be alive and limited.

In medicine and public health, the word is stripped of emotion and used with precision, but even there, underlying every mortality statistic is a human life lost.

• Mortality rate — how many people die per unit of a population in a given period
  • Infant/child/maternal mortality — death rates specific to those groups
  • Face/confront one's mortality — to be powerfully reminded that you will die
  • Come to terms with one's mortality — to accept and make peace with the fact of dying
  • Sense of mortality — a feeling or awareness of being temporary
  • Human mortality — the universal truth that all humans die
  • Mortality salience — a psychology term for the state of being made aware of death, and the behavioral effects that awareness triggers

Mortality, as a noun, carries two essential meanings that share one root truth — living things do not live forever:

1. Philosophically: It is the condition of being alive and temporary — the fact that all living beings are destined to die. This meaning is deeply personal and often tied to awareness, acceptance, and meaning.

2. Statistically: It is the rate or frequency of death within a given group, time, or context — a tool for measuring how many people die and from what causes.

Whether someone says "he was forced to confront his own mortality" or "the mortality rate declined," the word always points back to the same fundamental reality: life has an end, and mortality is the word we use to name that fact.
10727: The word mortar has three completely separate and distinct meanings in English. They share the same spelling but refer to three very different things. Think of them as three different words that just happen to look identical. Here they are, one by one.

This is probably the most common meaning.

What it is: Mortar is a thick, soft, paste-like mixture made by combining a binding material (such as cement or lime), sand, and water. When freshly made, it looks and feels a bit like very thick mud or putty — wet, sticky, and spreadable.

What it does: Its job is to act as an adhesive and gap-filler in construction. Bricklayers spread it between bricks, stones, concrete blocks, or tiles to hold them together. When mortar dries, it hardens into a solid, stone-like material, locking everything firmly in place.

How to picture it: Look at any brick wall — old or new. Do you see those thin lines running horizontally and vertically between every brick? Those lines are hardened mortar. The bricks would simply tumble apart without it. Mortar is the "glue" of masonry construction.

Mortar vs. concrete: Many learners confuse these two. Both involve cement, sand, and water, but they serve different purposes. Concrete is much thicker and stronger — it is used for big structural things like floors, pillars, beams, and foundations. Mortar is softer and more workable; it is specifically designed to sit in the narrow joints between bricks, tiles, or stones. You would not use mortar to build a floor, and you would not use concrete to lay bricks.

The mortar board: When a bricklayer is working, they keep a supply of fresh mortar nearby on a flat, square board called a mortar board (or hawk). They scoop mortar from this board onto the bricks as they work. This flat board is itself also called a "mortar board" — worth knowing because it gave its name to something else entirely (the academic graduation cap), which was named after it because of the resemblance in shape.

Common phrases you'll encounter:

  • "Applying mortar" — spreading it between bricks before laying them
  • "Pointing" or "repointing" — the process of repairing or renewing old, crumbling mortar in a wall
  • "Mortar joint" — the filled gap between two bricks or stones
  • "Brick and mortar" — a phrase meaning a physical, real-world building (like a shop you can walk into), as opposed to something that exists only online. For example: "They moved from a brick-and-mortar store to an online business."

This is the mortar that comes with a pestle, and the two are almost always mentioned together as a pair: "mortar and pestle."

What it is: A mortar (in this sense) is a small, sturdy, bowl-shaped container. It is typically made from hard materials — stone, marble, granite, ceramic, cast iron, or wood — because its job involves a lot of grinding and pounding. The pestle is the companion tool: a club-shaped or rounded stick that you hold in your hand and use to crush or grind substances inside the bowl.

The mortar is the bowl. The pestle is the stick.

What it does: You place ingredients inside the mortar and use the pestle to press, crush, pound, and grind them against the rough interior surface of the bowl. The result can be a fine powder, a coarse grind, or a smooth paste, depending on how long and how hard you work at it.

Where you see it:

  • In the kitchen: crushing whole spices like peppercorns, cardamom pods, cloves, cumin seeds; grinding fresh herbs; making chutneys, pastes, sauces. Dishes like pesto (Italian basil sauce) and guacamole are traditionally made in a mortar and pestle. Indian cooking uses it constantly for grinding masalas and spice pastes.
  • In pharmacy and medicine: Before modern machines, pharmacists and apothecaries used mortars and pestles to grind medicinal ingredients into powders or mix them into pastes. Even today, the mortar and pestle is the universal symbol of pharmacy — you'll see it on pharmacy signs and logos around the world.
  • In science and chemistry laboratories: for grinding solid materials into fine powders for experiments.

Important distinction: The mortar is passive — it is just the bowl that sits on the table. The pestle is the active tool you use. But the word "mortar" always refers to the bowl, never the stick.

This mortar is something completely different: a weapon.

What it is: A mortar is a short, wide, tube-shaped weapon — essentially a type of portable cannon or artillery piece — used by armies to fire explosive shells over long distances. It consists of a smooth metal tube (the barrel), an angled base plate that sits on the ground, and supporting legs. It is small enough to be carried and set up by a small team of soldiers.

How it works: A soldier drops a specialized explosive shell (called a mortar round or mortar bomb) into the open top of the tube. The shell slides down, hits a firing pin at the bottom, and is launched up and out. The key feature that distinguishes a mortar from other weapons is its firing angle — it shoots shells at a very steep, high angle, almost straight up into the sky. The shell arcs high into the air in a curved path and then comes straight down onto the target.

Why this matters: Because the shell travels in a steep, high arc, it can hit targets that a direct-fire weapon (like a rifle or a flat-shooting cannon) cannot reach — for example, enemy soldiers hiding behind a hill, a wall, a building, or in a trench. The shell sails over the obstacle and falls down onto whatever is on the other side. This makes mortars extremely useful in combat situations where the enemy is out of direct line of sight.

Key characteristics:

  • Lightweight and portable — a small crew can carry it and set it up quickly anywhere on a battlefield.
  • Short barrel — much shorter than a traditional cannon or artillery gun.
  • High arc — fires at angles typically between 45 and 85 degrees (nearly vertical).
  • Used for indirect fire — meaning you fire at a target you cannot directly see.

When you hear it in context: In news reports, war films, or history books, phrases like "mortar fire," "mortar attack," "mortar rounds," "mortar shelling," or "under mortar bombardment" all refer to this weapon being used. The sound of an incoming mortar shell is often described as a distinctive whistle followed by a loud explosion.
How to keep all three meanings apart

If it helps, think of them in three simple mental images:

Mortar #1 (construction): Picture the grey lines between bricks in a wall. That grey stuff holding everything together — that is mortar.

Mortar #2 (kitchen/pharmacy): Picture a heavy stone bowl sitting on a kitchen counter, with someone grinding spices in it with a rounded stone stick. The bowl is the mortar.

Mortar #3 (military): Picture a short metal tube propped up at an angle in the ground, with a soldier dropping a shell into it. That tube is a mortar.

The context in which you encounter the word will almost always make it crystal clear which mortar is meant.
10728:
A mortgage is a loan you take out to buy property — most commonly a house — where the property itself acts as the bank's guarantee that you'll pay the money back. If you stop making payments, the bank has the legal right to take the property from you to recover what it's owed.

That's the heart of it. Everything else is just detail around this idea.
A Real-Life Example to Make It Click

Imagine you want to buy a house that costs $300,000. You have $30,000 saved up. You don't have the other $270,000, so you go to a bank and ask to borrow it. The bank agrees, but it doesn't just hand you money and trust you blindly. Instead, it says: "We'll lend you this money, but we want the house itself as security. If you ever stop paying us back, the house becomes ours."

You agree. You sign the mortgage. Now you get to move into the house and live in it, but the bank holds a legal claim over it until you've paid back every dollar — plus interest. Once you've made your final payment, that legal claim disappears and the house is truly, fully yours.

That loan agreement — the entire arrangement between you and the bank — is called a mortgage.

The principal is the actual amount of money you borrowed — in the example above, that's $270,000. This is what you are fundamentally obligated to pay back.

The interest is the bank's fee for lending you the money. Banks are businesses; they don't lend for free. Interest is calculated as a percentage of the outstanding loan amount each year (called the interest rate). So if your interest rate is 6%, you owe 6% of your remaining balance as a fee each year, on top of repaying the principal itself.

The monthly payment is what you pay the bank every single month, which is a blend of two things: part of it chips away at the principal (reducing what you owe), and part of it covers the interest for that month. Early in a mortgage, most of your monthly payment goes toward interest because you still owe so much. Over time, as the principal shrinks, more and more of each payment goes toward the principal.

The term is the length of time you have agreed to pay the mortgage back over. Common terms are 15 years or 30 years. A longer term means smaller monthly payments, but you end up paying significantly more in total interest over time. A shorter term means higher monthly payments, but you pay far less in total interest and own your home sooner.

The down payment is the money you pay upfront out of your own pocket. It is not part of the mortgage — it's your initial contribution. The larger your down payment, the less you need to borrow, and therefore the smaller your mortgage.

Collateral is the financial concept that makes a mortgage special. The property you're buying is pledged as security — meaning the bank has a legal right (called a lien) over the house until the debt is fully cleared. This is what separates a mortgage from a regular personal loan.

Equity is the portion of the home you genuinely "own" at any point in time. If your home is worth $300,000 and you still owe the bank $200,000, then you have $100,000 in equity. As you pay down the mortgage, your equity grows. If the market value of the home rises, your equity rises too.
What Happens If You Stop Paying

If a borrower stops making mortgage payments and fails to catch up, the bank initiates a process called foreclosure. This is when the lender legally takes possession of the property and sells it to recover the unpaid debt. Foreclosure is a serious, life-altering consequence, which is why it's important never to take on a mortgage you cannot realistically afford to repay.

Fixed-rate mortgage: The interest rate is locked in at the start and stays the same for the entire term. Your monthly payment never changes, which makes budgeting predictable and stable. Most people prefer this type.

Adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM): The interest rate is fixed for an initial period (say, 5 years), then fluctuates periodically based on broader market interest rates. Your monthly payment can go up or down. This type can be risky if rates rise sharply.

Interest-only mortgage: For a set period, you only pay the interest each month and pay nothing toward the principal. Payments are lower upfront, but you're not actually reducing the debt at all during that period. Eventually, you must start paying down the principal, which significantly raises payments.

Reverse mortgage: A special product designed for older homeowners (typically 62+) who already own their homes. Instead of you paying the bank each month, the bank pays you — essentially letting you convert your home's equity into cash. The loan is repaid when the homeowner sells the house, moves out permanently, or passes away.
How Mortgage Payments Are Structured Over Time

The process of gradually paying off a mortgage through regular payments is called amortization. Here's the important insight: even though your monthly payment stays the same (on a fixed-rate mortgage), the split between interest and principal changes every month.

Early on, interest takes up most of your payment because your outstanding balance is large. Month by month, as the balance shrinks, the interest portion gets smaller and the principal portion gets larger. By the time you're in the final years of a 30-year mortgage, almost your entire monthly payment is going straight toward the principal. It's a slow, front-heavy process by design.
Common Ways the Word Is Used

"She applied for a mortgage to buy her first flat." — The loan itself.

"They've been paying off their mortgage for twelve years." — Referring to the ongoing repayment process.

"The bank denied his mortgage application." — A request for such a loan.

"Once we pay off the mortgage, the house is fully ours." — Completion of the agreement.

"They fell behind on the mortgage and feared losing the home." — Monthly payment obligations.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

A mortgage is not just a loan — it's a secured loan. The security is the property itself. That one feature — the fact that the lender has a claim on your home until every penny is repaid — is what defines a mortgage and distinguishes it from every other type of borrowing. It's what makes lenders willing to give you hundreds of thousands of dollars at relatively low interest rates, and it's what makes defaulting on a mortgage so serious.
10729: To mortgage something means to formally pledge something valuable you own as a guarantee for a loan or obligation — while knowingly accepting that if you fail to meet that obligation, you risk losing the thing you pledged.

Think of it this way. Imagine you need money urgently, and someone is willing to lend it to you — but they want assurance that you'll pay them back. You say: "I'll use my house as a guarantee. If I don't repay you, you can take my house." That act of pledging your house as that guarantee is mortgaging it.

You haven't sold the house. You still live in it, own it, and use it as you normally would. But it now carries a legal claim against it — a burden — that remains until you fully repay what you owe. The moment you finish repaying, the claim lifts and the asset is fully yours again. But if you fail to repay, the lender has the legal right to seize it.

In its most direct sense, you mortgage a physical asset — almost always property like a house or land — to secure a loan from a bank or lender.

"He mortgaged his farmland to borrow money for the new machinery."

This means he went to a lender and said: "I want to borrow money. I am using my farmland as collateral. If I cannot repay you, the land is yours." The lender agreed and disbursed the money, and the farmland now serves as the security backing that agreement.

Notice what mortgaging is not: it is not selling. When you sell something, you surrender it immediately in exchange for money — it's gone. When you mortgage something, you keep it, but you place a conditional legal claim on it. The thing is yours as long as you hold up your end. The risk is real but not yet realized.

This is where the verb becomes truly expressive and you'll encounter it most often in everyday language. Used figuratively, to mortgage something means to trade away a future benefit, freedom, or resource in exchange for something you want or need right now.

"By spending recklessly, the government has mortgaged the future of its citizens."

No property is involved here. But the logic is identical: you are getting something now and placing the burden of payment on your future self — or in this case, future generations. The future is "pledged." Eventually, just like a real mortgage, the bill comes due.

"She mortgaged her health by sleeping only four hours a night for years to build her career."

She gained success in the present, but placed her long-term health at risk to get it. She "pledged" her future wellbeing as the price of present achievement.

The figurative use almost always carries a note of caution or warning. When someone says something is being "mortgaged," they're drawing attention to the fact that a future cost is being quietly accumulated — one that may be painful or irreversible when it finally arrives.
The Two Things That Make This Word Distinct

Understanding "mortgage" as a verb depends on grasping two things that set it apart from similar words like "borrow" or "risk."

First, there is a specific asset on the line. When you mortgage something, it's not a vague promise — a particular, identifiable thing is pledged. The lender (or the future, in the figurative sense) has a claim on that specific thing. This makes the stakes concrete and defined.

Second, you retain possession while the risk hangs over you. This is what makes mortgaging psychologically distinct. You are not giving anything up immediately. Life continues. You use the house, you enjoy the career, the country runs its budget. But all along, there is a clock ticking and a claim waiting to be settled. The loss is not certain, but it is possible — and it grows more likely the longer you fail to meet the obligation.

To mortgage something is to say: "I will use something I value as a pledge to get what I need now, and I accept that I must pay a future price — or risk losing what I pledged." Whether the pledge is a house offered to a bank, or a generation's financial freedom spent by politicians today, or a person's health traded for short-term success, the verb always carries the same weight: a valuable thing is staked against a future obligation, and the cost will eventually come due.
